meta.title: Who really said "Foolish the doctor who despises knowledge acquired by the ancients"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No Hippocratic treatise carries this sentence. The idea is genuine — On Ancient Medicine warns against despising older discoveries — the wording is not.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Foolish the doctor who despises knowledge acquired by the ancients'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in the Hippocratic corpus. The idea is real — On Ancient Medicine condemns “rejecting and despising” older discoveries — but the wording is modern.

answer.label: Not a Hippocratic text — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos
answer.sourceLine: No treatise in the Hippocratic corpus produces this sentence in the standard English translations, and no primary source for the wording has been located — of the aggregators we could check, only one attaches a label at all, and that label is a 1984 popular book on childbirth. The argument, though, is genuinely Hippocratic: On Ancient Medicine holds that whoever rejects and despises medicine’s inherited discoveries “is deceived himself and deceives others.”

source.heading: What the Hippocratic text actually says

docMeta.dd: No primary source located — absent from the Hippocratic corpus in English translation. It usually circulates with the definite article: “despises the knowledge acquired by the ancients.”
Francis Adams, The Genuine Works of Hippocrates (Sydenham Society, London, 1849)
Michel Odent, Entering the World (1984) — a modern book, not a Greek text

source.excerpt: But all these requisites belong of old to Medicine, and an origin and way have been found out, by which many and elegant discoveries have been made, during a length of time… But whoever, rejecting and despising all these, attempts to pursue another course and form of inquiry, and says he has discovered anything, is deceived himself and deceives others, for the thing is impossible.
trail: The line runs on quote aggregators with no source behind it: AZQuotes ↗ names no work, translation or date — only the label “Entering the world (M. Odent).”
Wikiquote’s Hippocrates page ↗ does not list the sentence anywhere; its nearest entry is the “ancient Art” passage from On Ancient Medicine in Francis Adams’ translation.
A site search of Quote Investigator ↗ returns no article on this line, so there is no specialist tracing to defer to — and no earlier attestation on record anywhere we could find.
The genuine argument sits in On Ancient Medicine, part 2 ↗, which condemns “rejecting and despising” the discoveries medicine had already made.
source.excerptNote: Part 12 of the same treatise puts it plainly: “we ought not to reject the ancient Art… but rather… to receive it and admire its discoveries.” Neither passage yields the sentence that circulates under Hippocrates’ name.
source.rightsNote: Rights follow the work, and no work has been identified for this wording, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The passage excerpted above is a different sentence: it comes from Francis Adams’ translation of On Ancient Medicine, first issued by the Sydenham Society in London in 1849, and is long in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: Hippocrates of Kos
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos, called the Father of Medicine
author.bio: Hippocrates was a Greek physician and philosopher of the classical period, born on the island of Kos and traditionally called the Father of Medicine. Very little is known concretely about what he himself thought, wrote or did: the sixty-odd treatises that travel under his name were gathered later, and none of them is proven to be his. That gap is exactly why his name attracts quotations — a maxim about medicine sounds authoritative the moment it is signed “Hippocrates,” and almost nobody checks.

misattribution.heading: What is actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: Nothing about this line is malicious, and the sentiment really is Hippocratic. What is missing is the sentence.

items.why: No treatise in the corpus produces this sentence in the standard English translations — not On Ancient Medicine ↗, not Precepts ↗ — and Wikiquote ↗ does not carry it in any section, sourced, attributed or misattributed.

items.scope: The one source label anyone offers
items.why: Of the aggregators we could check, AZQuotes ↗ is the only one that attaches anything at all, and what it attaches is the label “Entering the world (M. Odent)” — a popular work on childbirth published in New York in 1984 ↗. That is a twentieth-century obstetrician quoting Hippocrates, not a Hippocratic source, and whether the book even contains the sentence is unconfirmed.
Even for genuine passages the credit is loose: none of the texts in the corpus ↗ is proven to be by Hippocrates himself, though On Ancient Medicine is among those listed as possibly genuine.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: the thought is in On Ancient Medicine, part 2 ↗, which warns that whoever rejects and despises medicine’s inherited discoveries “is deceived himself and deceives others” — but the tidy one-liner is somebody else’s English.

context.heading: The argument the proverb compresses
lead: On Ancient Medicine is a polemic, not a book of maxims. Its author is arguing against physicians who wanted to rebuild the whole of medicine on a single first principle — hot, cold, wet, dry — and discard the accumulated craft of diet, regimen and bedside observation. His answer is that the old art was arrived at by long trial and error, that it has produced “many and elegant discoveries,” and that anyone who throws it out and announces a fresh discovery is fooling himself and everyone else.

That is a real position with a real target, which is why the modern one-liner lands so well: it is not inventing a sentiment out of nothing. It compresses several paragraphs of fifth-century BC argument into a proverb — and then puts the proverb inside quotation marks and signs it.
detailsBody: A small tell in the English: “Foolish the doctor who…” is verbless, a construction that reads like a literal rendering out of another language rather than like any of the standard English Hippocratic translations, which are uniformly full-sentence Victorian or Loeb prose. That is an observation about style, not evidence of an origin — but it fits a line that surfaces with a French author’s book as its only label.

It is worth separating two questions that quote sites collapse. Whether the Hippocratic corpus says something like this: yes, clearly. Whether Hippocrates the man wrote it: unknowable, since none of the corpus is securely his. Whether this string of English words comes from either: no.
context.pull: The sentiment survives the fact-check. The sentence does not.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Hippocrates page does not contain "Foolish the doctor who despises knowledge acquired by the ancients" in any section; its nearest entry is the "we ought not to reject the ancient Art" passage from On Ancient Medicine in Francis Adams' translation.

On Ancient Medicine, part 2, in Francis Adams' translation reads: "But whoever, rejecting and despising all these, attempts to pursue another course and form of inquiry, and says he has discovered anything, is deceived himself and deceives others, for the thing is impossible."
The Internet Classics Archive hosts On Ancient Medicine by Hippocrates, translated by Francis Adams; the complete text contains no sentence resembling the popular quotation.

The full text of On Ancient Medicine (Adams) contains, in part 12: "But on that account, I say, we ought not to reject the ancient Art, as if it were not, and had not been properly founded... but rather... to receive it and admire its discoveries."
Perseus hosts Hippocrates' Praeceptiones (Precepts) in W. H. S. Jones' Loeb translation; the fourteen sections contain no sentence about a doctor despising knowledge acquired by the ancients.
AZQuotes carries the quotation and attaches no book, translation or date to it, showing only the label "Entering the world (M. Odent)".
Michel Odent's Entering the World: The De-Medicalization of Childbirth was published in New York by New American Library in 1984.
Francis Adams' The Genuine Works of Hippocrates was originally issued by the Sydenham Society, London, 1849.
A site search of Quote Investigator for Hippocrates returns no article investigating "Foolish the doctor who despises knowledge acquired by the ancients".
None of the texts in the Hippocratic Corpus is proven to be by Hippocrates himself, and On Ancient Medicine is listed among the works described as possibly genuine.

Hippocrates lived c. 460 – c. 370 BC, was a Greek physician and philosopher of the classical period from the island of Kos, and very little is known concretely about what he himself thought, wrote and did.
